newsitem.title: USA: N. Carolina Senate panel approves $1 bln bond deal.
newsitem.headline: N. Carolina Senate panel approves $1 bln bond deal.

text.p: A North Carolina Senate panel has approved a $1 billion general obligation bond issue for water and sewer projects, which would be the state's third major GO authorization in a little over a year.
The proposal, sponsored by Sen. John Kerr, D-Wayne, was approved Tuesday by the Senate Finance Committee. If approved by the General Assembly, it would go before voters in November.

Eighty percent of bond proceeds would be available to cities and counties to upgrade water, sewer and waste treatment systems. It would enable them to reduce borrowing costs by taking advantage of the state's triple-A bond rating.
The remaining proceeds would be used to boost the state's revolving loan fund for clean water projects.

A study by the North Carolina rural Economic Development Center said the state needs to spend abut $11.3 billion over the next 20 years to update local water and sewer systems, any of which have not been upgraded in 50 years.

The proposal would be the third major statewide GO bond authorization in a little over a year. North Carolina voters approved $1.8 billion of general obligation bonds for school construction and $950 million of highway GOs in November.

State Treasurer Harlan Boyles said Wednesday that North Carolina could incur the additional debt without jeopardizing its AAA rating. But he encouraged lawmakers to consider the overall effect before approving the plan.
"While we would anticipate repayment from the localities, there still is a contingent liability there on the part of the state," Boyles said.

"I think there's a capacity to incur the debt without a real risk. The problem is, once the debt is incurred, what impact does the total debt of the state have on future resources of the state, and to what extent would those future demands displace scarce dollars?" Boyles asked.

"We have to understand that this kind of debt cannot be incurred without utilizing future resources of the state," Boyles said. "It's necessary that we look at all the demands on the state's resources and not move each of them forward on their individual merits without knowing the consequences of the total."
